..
Issued at 240 AM CDT Mon Oct 12 2026

A 500-hPa analysis shows mid-level ridging present over the  
central CONUS, with a high amplitude trough situated over the 
western CONUS and a shortwave along the East Coast. This pattern
will continue to support near, or above, record temperatures 
today, with highs expected to be in the upper 80s and low 90s. 
At the surface, a frontal boundary is draped from the Upper 
Great Lakes back to a low pressure system that is developing in 
northeast CO and the NE panhandle. A broad area of high pressure
is situated over the Gulf Coast. A tight pressure gradient 
between these two surface features will allow breezy (10-15 mph)
southwesterly winds to continue through the early morning hours
this morning across northern MO and northeastern KS with gusts 
up to 25 mph possible at times. The low pressure system is 
expected to move northeast through the day today, further 
tightening the pressure gradient and allowing winds to increase 
to 15-20 mph by the afternoon with gusts up to 35 mph. While the
winds alone create elevated fire weather concerns given the dry
antecedent conditions, afternoon RHs will only fall to the 
35-50% range, so Red Flag Criteria is not expected to be met 
today.

As the low pressure system moves towards the Upper Great Lakes
today, it will push a cold front across NE and IA. This front is
expected to reach northwest MO this evening/overnight. The nose
of a 30-35 kt LLJ will reach into southeastern NE and
northwestern MO overnight, which may provide enough lift for a
few showers to form along or behind the front through the early
morning hours.

The progression of the front is expected to slow on Tuesday, 
with the front becoming nearly stationary across northern MO. 
Model guidance remain in poor agreement on where exactly this 
stall will happen, resulting in large spreads in forecast 
temperatures on Tuesday. However, the general consensus is for 
areas south of the front to be in the low 90s (making Tuesday 
the hottest day of this heat wave), while areas north of the 
front will see temperatures in the low-to-mid 80s. Southerly 
surface flow will also continue on Tuesday bringing Gulf 
moisture into the region. Dew points are expected to climb into
the upper 60s and low 70s by Tuesday afternoon, which will 
actually bring heat indices in the upper 90s to near 100F into 
play, which is mind-boggling for mid-October.

Another result of the influx of boundary layer moisture will be
the development of 1000-2000 J/kg of MLCAPE south of the frontal
boundary Tuesday afternoon/evening. This will come in
conjunction with 40-50 kts of deep layer shear. To the west, a
mid-level trough will slide east over the Great Basin and lee
cyclogenesis will occur in southeastern CO. With better synoptic
support focused to the west of the local area, CAM guidance 
indicates that convective initiation should occur across central
KS and areas south by mid-afternoon. The local area will be 
capped through much of the afternoon, however, the combination 
of diurnal heating and increasing synoptic support should allow 
the cap to erode through the day and convection appears likely 
along the frontal boundary by late afternoon/early evening. Mid-
level lapse rates are not overly impressive (6.5-7 C/km), 
however, given the parameter space previously outlined, strong 
to severe storms appear possible, with the primary threats being
damaging winds and hail up to 1" in diameter. This thinking 
aligns with the SPC Day 2 outlook, which outlines eastern KS and
western MO in a Slight (Level 2 of 5) Risk with the remainder 
of northern MO in a Marginal (Level 1 of 5) Risk.

Continued ascent along the frontal boundary Tuesday night will 
lead to the development of widespread showers and storms by 
early Wednesday morning, lasting into Thursday. The presence of
this precipitation makes the convective forecast for Wednesday 
a little uncertain. Model guidance indicates that at least some 
instability will be present, with shear values remaining 
elevated, so it seems as though at least some severe threat 
exists Wednesday afternoon/evening, though, the best parameter 
space should be on the southern periphery of the showers. SPC 
has outlined the far southern portion of the CWA in a Day 3 
Marginal (Level 1 of 5) Risk, which matches this thinking.

Though model guidance diverges on the handling of the upper 
trough beyond Thursday, there is agreement that a cold front 
will sweep across the Central Plains Thursday afternoon/evening
and high pressure will build in from the northwest bringing a
cool down to the region. The current forecast calls for highs 
in the upper 50s and low 60s on Friday and Saturday with low 
falling into the 30s on Friday night.
